scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a claim response that backs limits on power while arguing a strict five-year rule is too rigid; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: History warns us how dangerous it is when one person holds power for too long.
Some people claim that those in power, in any profession, should step down after five years.
I agree that limiting time in power can be healthy, but I believe a strict five-year rule would also cause harm.
First, limiting how long people hold power can prevent serious abuse.
Leaders who stay too long may grow arrogant and stop listening to anyone around them.
For example, rulers who cling to power for decades often become corrupt and difficult to remove.
This shows that regular change can protect an organisation from one person's worst faults.
Fresh leaders also bring new ideas and energy that long rule tends to drain away.
Knowing their time is limited can keep those in power humble and focused.
To this extent, limiting time in power is a sensible idea.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why a rigid rule is too strict

sentences.text: Second, however, forcing everyone to step down after exactly five years would be too rigid.
Some roles require many years of experience before a person can perform them really well.
Consider a skilled leader removed just as she has finally mastered a difficult and complex job.
Such a rule would throw away valuable experience at the very moment it becomes most useful.
A fixed limit also ignores that some leaders keep serving honestly and effectively for far longer.
Constant forced change can leave an organisation unstable and always starting over.
Limits on power, then, work best when they are sensible rather than rigidly fixed.
In conclusion, limiting time in power can guard against arrogance and abuse.
But a strict five-year rule for everyone would waste experience and create instability.
The wiser approach sets fair limits on power without forcing out every leader at the same fixed moment.
